acl.name: ACL Tear
acl.performanceLabel: Significant decrease in targets, receptions, yards, TDs vs. pre-injury
acl.careerImpact: Career shortened by ~1.9 seasons vs. matched controls
acl.fantasyImpact: Dynasty value typically drops 40-60% immediately. Year 1 back averages WR30-40 production. Year 2 bounce is real but inconsistent.

achilles.name: Achilles Tear
achilles.returnRateLabel: Only 38% of WRs return (lowest of all positions)
achilles.performanceLabel: 88% reduction in power ratings over 3 years post-injury for WRs
achilles.careerImpact: Most career-threatening injury for skill players. Average of 1 additional NFL season if they return.
achilles.fantasyImpact: Dynasty value craters 70-80%. Most WRs never return to fantasy relevance. TEs have slightly better outcomes (~55% return rate).
achilles.sources: American Journal of Sports Medicine, British Journal of Sports Medicine

concussion.name: Concussion
concussion.reinjuryLabel: 5.3–8.3% same-season repeat risk after first concussion
concussion.performanceLabel: No significant acute performance decline in most studies
concussion.careerImpact: Players with 3+ concussions have elevated retirement risk. WRs 70% more likely to report long-term cognitive impairment (Harvard FPHS).
concussion.fantasyImpact: Minimal short-term fantasy impact. Long-term dynasty concern only if pattern develops (3+ career concussions). Monitor contested catch rate as a risk indicator.
concussion.sources: Neurosurgery (2022), Harvard Football Players Health Study, OJSM

hamstring.name: Hamstring Strain
hamstring.reinjuryLabel: 12–33% recurrence rate within first year (highest of any soft tissue injury)
hamstring.performanceLabel: Minimal production impact once fully healed. Main risk is the re-aggravation cycle.
hamstring.careerImpact: Not career-threatening on its own. Becomes a pattern concern when recurring — can lead to chronic management situations.
hamstring.fantasyImpact: Short-term: miss 1-4 games. Long-term dynasty concern only if recurrence pattern develops. Speed-dependent WRs (4.4 or faster) are higher recurrence risk.
hamstring.sources: BJSM hamstring meta-analyses, NFL injury data

high_ankle.name: High Ankle Sprain
high_ankle.performanceLabel: Significant impact on WR route-running and RB cutting ability. Residual effects 2-4 weeks after return.
high_ankle.careerImpact: Not career-threatening. But WRs playing through high ankle sprains show measurably decreased separation and burst metrics.
high_ankle.fantasyImpact: Expect 3-6 weeks missed. When player returns, discount production ~20% for 2-3 weeks. High ankle sprains are more impactful than low ankle sprains for skill players.
high_ankle.sources: Return to Play After Isolated Syndesmotic Ligamentous Injury in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, OJSM (2022); Corticosteroid Injections Hasten Return to Play of NFL Players Following Stable Ankle Syndesmosis Sprains, OJSM (2015); Miller et al, comparative time-loss for syndesmotic vs lateral ankle sprains in professional football

turf_toe.name: Turf Toe (Grade 3)
turf_toe.returnRateLabel: ~80% return, but often with lingering issues
turf_toe.reinjuryLabel: ~20% chance of chronic issues requiring additional procedures
turf_toe.performanceLabel: Affects push-off and acceleration. QBs lose mobility, WRs lose burst off the line.
turf_toe.careerImpact: Grade 3 (complete plantar plate tear) is significantly worse than Grade 1-2. Can become a chronic issue if not managed properly.
turf_toe.fantasyImpact: Expect 8-16 weeks missed. QBs often play through but with reduced mobility. Dynasty impact moderate — usually not career-ending but can linger for years.
turf_toe.sources: The Effect of Turf Toe Injuries on Player Performance in the National Football League, Foot & Ankle International (2020); Smith & Waldrop, Operative Outcomes of Grade 3 Turf Toe Injuries in Competitive Football Players, Foot & Ankle International (2018); Return to Play Following High-Grade Turf Toe Injuries in NFL Athletes, Orthopaedic Journal at Harvard Medical School (2021)

pcl.name: PCL Tear
pcl.reinjuryLabel: Lower re-tear risk than ACL, but affects deceleration long-term
pcl.performanceLabel: Affects deceleration and cutting. Less devastating than ACL but still impactful for skill players.
pcl.careerImpact: Better prognosis than ACL. Many players return to full production. Main concern is combined ligament damage.
pcl.fantasyImpact: Dynasty discount of 20-30%. Most players return to near-prior production within one season. The key variable is whether other structures were also damaged.

mcl.name: MCL Sprain
mcl.avgReturn: Grade I ~13.5 days; Grade II–III ~29 days
mcl.returnRateLabel: Nearly all return; isolated grade I–II are treated without surgery
mcl.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence not separately reported in the elite-football literature
mcl.performanceLabel: Low grades are frequently played through in a brace; no published NFL performance drop
mcl.careerImpact: Isolated MCL injury is not career-altering. Combined with an ACL tear it is, and the ACL drives that.
mcl.fantasyImpact: The knee injury you want. A grade I is often a one-to-two-game absence; a grade II runs three to five. Grade III, or any MCL alongside another ligament, is a different conversation entirely.
mcl.sources: Lundblad et al, UEFA Elite Club Injury Study — 130 MCL injuries of 4,364 registered, KSSTA (2019); Return to Play After Medial Collateral Ligament Injury (2016)

meniscus.name: Meniscus Tear
meniscus.returnRateLabel: 80–86% of elite athletes return after operative treatment
meniscus.reinjuryLabel: Cartilage damage is the longer-term risk: 85% of NFL prospects with a prior meniscectomy had a chondral lesion on imaging
meniscus.performanceLabel: Combine metrics were inferior in both the repair and meniscectomy groups
meniscus.careerImpact: The operation matters more than the tear. A trim is weeks and costs meniscus you never get back; a repair is months and keeps it.
meniscus.fantasyImpact: Ask which surgery. 'Meniscus' with a two-to-six-week timeline is a trim and he plays this season; a repair is a redshirt. American football was the most common sport in the elite-athlete literature.
meniscus.sources: Systematic review of operative meniscal tears in elite athletes, JISAKOS (2021); Brophy et al, Meniscectomy and Resultant Articular Cartilage Lesions Among Prospective NFL Players, AJSM (2017)

low_ankle.name: Low Ankle Sprain
low_ankle.returnRateLabel: 91% of all NFL ankle injuries return to play
low_ankle.reinjuryLabel: Up to 70% develop some chronic instability after recurrent sprains
low_ankle.performanceLabel: Little measured short-term effect; the risk is accumulation, not the single event
low_ankle.careerImpact: One is nothing. Recurrent instability is what eventually forces retirements, despite an initial return.
low_ankle.fantasyImpact: The most over-panicked injury on the report. A rolled ankle costs a fraction of a game on average — roughly a quarter of what a high ankle sprain costs. Check which one it is before you sell.
low_ankle.sources: Epidemiology and Outcomes of Ankle Injuries in the National Football League, OJSM (2022); Miller et al, comparative time-loss for syndesmotic vs lateral ankle sprains in professional football

ac_joint.name: AC Joint Sprain
ac_joint.returnRateLabel: Over 98% treated without surgery and return
ac_joint.performanceLabel: No study has measured performance after AC injury specifically; other shoulder injuries show no measurable drop
ac_joint.careerImpact: Not career-altering. 96% of NFL cases are low-grade types I and II.
ac_joint.fantasyImpact: A shoulder separation sounds worse than it plays. It is the most common shoulder injury in the league and costs a game or two — except at quarterback, where the throwing shoulder roughly doubles the absence.
ac_joint.sources: Lynch et al, Acromioclavicular joint injuries in the National Football League: epidemiology and management, NFL Injury Surveillance System 2000–2011 (2013)

shoulder_instability.name: Shoulder Dislocation / Instability
shoulder_instability.avgReturn: Subluxation ~0 weeks; dislocation ~3 weeks; after surgery ~39 weeks
shoulder_instability.returnRateLabel: 92% of NFL players return to regular-season play
shoulder_instability.reinjuryLabel: 47% suffer a recurrent instability event — 26% after surgical repair against 55% without it
shoulder_instability.performanceLabel: Not separately measured in the NFL cohort
shoulder_instability.careerImpact: The first one rarely ends anything. The pattern of recurrence is what does.
shoulder_instability.fantasyImpact: He will probably not miss a game — and will probably do it again. Half of these recur, and a player who chooses surgery is gone for the season but far less likely to repeat it.
shoulder_instability.sources: Return to play after shoulder instability in National Football League athletes, Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (2017)

pectoral.name: Pectoralis Major Tear
pectoral.returnRateLabel: 83–86% of NFL players return after surgical repair
pectoral.reinjuryLabel: Re-rupture not separately reported in the NFL cohort
pectoral.performanceLabel: A performance drop appears overall but disappears once players are matched for position and draft capital
pectoral.careerImpact: Incidence has risen sharply — only 10 complete ruptures were recorded across 2000–2010.
pectoral.fantasyImpact: A season, not a stretch. Ten months means an in-season tear is a full redshirt, and defensive linemen and receivers are the groups whose production has been shown to suffer on return.
pectoral.sources: Farooq et al, Surgically Treated Pectoralis Major Tears Impact the Play and Performance of NFL Athletes, Arthroscopy Sports Medicine & Rehabilitation (2022); Pectoralis Major Ruptures in the NFL: Incidence, RTP, and Performance Analysis, OJSM (2021)

lisfranc.name: Lisfranc Injury
lisfranc.returnRateLabel: 81.8–83% of NFL players return to play
lisfranc.performanceLabel: Statistically significant fall in Approximate Value in the return year; offensive players decline more than defensive
lisfranc.careerImpact: Most return, but the year they come back is measurably worse than the year before.
lisfranc.fantasyImpact: Season-ending, and the following season is not a clean slate — the measured decline lands in the return year. Running backs and offensive linemen account for the largest share of these.
lisfranc.sources: Abed et al, Return to Play, Performance, and Economic Analysis of National Football League Players After Lisfranc Injury, OJSM (2023); Performance-Based Outcomes Following Lisfranc Injury Among Professional American Football and Rugby Athletes (2018)

adductor.name: Groin / Adductor Strain
adductor.avgReturn: Most return inside a week; a rectus femoris avulsion runs 6–12 weeks
adductor.returnRateLabel: Return rate not separately reported; nearly all return
adductor.reinjuryLabel: ~6% recur in the first match back, with risk elevated for 15 weeks after return
adductor.careerImpact: Rarely career-altering on its own; the pattern of repeat strains is the problem.
adductor.fantasyImpact: The second most common strain in the league after the hamstring — 21% of all time-loss lower-body strains. Usually a week, but the recurrence window runs three months, so a second one in the same season is normal rather than surprising.
adductor.sources: Herzog et al, Lower Extremity Strains in the US National Football League 2015–2019, AJSM (2023); Orchard et al, Fifteen-week window for recurrent muscle strains, BJSM (2020)

quad.name: Quad Strain
quad.avgReturn: Typically 1–3 weeks; a rectus femoris avulsion 6–12 weeks
quad.returnRateLabel: Return rate not separately reported; nearly all return
quad.reinjuryLabel: ~5% recur in the first match back, elevated for 15 weeks
quad.fantasyImpact: The least common of the four big lower-body strains — 8% of the NFL's time-loss total — and the least likely to recur immediately. Usually a shorter absence than a hamstring of the same grade.
quad.sources: Herzog et al, Lower Extremity Strains in the US National Football League 2015–2019, AJSM (2023); Orchard et al, BJSM (2020)

calf.name: Calf Strain
calf.returnRateLabel: Return rate not separately reported; nearly all return
calf.reinjuryLabel: ~2% recur in the first match back — the lowest immediate recurrence of the major strains
calf.careerImpact: Not career-altering, though it skews to older players.
calf.fantasyImpact: 12% of the league's time-loss lower-body strains and the least likely to recur straight away. The worry is the Achilles above it — a calf complaint in an older player is worth watching rather than ignoring.
calf.sources: Herzog et al, Lower Extremity Strains in the US National Football League 2015–2019, AJSM (2023); Orchard et al, BJSM (2020)

disc.name: Lumbar Disc Herniation
disc.avgReturn: Non-operative often under a game; after discectomy, months
disc.returnRateLabel: 82% of NFL athletes return; 74% after lumbar discectomy
disc.performanceLabel: No significant difference between pre- and post-operative performance score across the remaining career
disc.careerImpact: Average career length after the injury is about 3.4 years. Surgically treated players had LONGER post-treatment careers than those managed without surgery.
disc.fantasyImpact: Sounds career-threatening and usually is not — but it caps how long he has left rather than how good he is. Performance holds up; the remaining career is what shortens.
disc.sources: Hsu et al, The Professional Athlete Spine Initiative: outcomes after lumbar disc herniation in 342 elite professional athletes, The Spine Journal (2011); Statistical performance in NFL athletes after lumbar discectomy (2010)

hip_labrum.name: Hip Labrum Tear / FAI
hip_labrum.avgReturn: Months after arthroscopy; not reported as a single figure for the NFL
hip_labrum.returnRateLabel: 87% of professional football hip arthroscopies returned to play
hip_labrum.reinjuryLabel: Revision rate not separately reported in the NFL cohort
hip_labrum.performanceLabel: Return rates vary by position — linemen were significantly less likely to return
hip_labrum.careerImpact: Position decides it. The same operation reads very differently for a lineman than for a skill player.
hip_labrum.fantasyImpact: Rarely reported by name — it hides behind 'hip' on the injury report. High return rates for skill positions, but the surgery costs most of a season when it happens.
hip_labrum.sources: Femoroacetabular Impingement in Professional Football Players: Return to Play and Predictors of Career Length After Hip Arthroscopy, Arthroscopy (2017); Hip Arthroscopy for Labral Tears and FAI in Professional American Football Athletes, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine (2024)

stinger.name: Stinger / Burner
stinger.avgReturn: Most miss no time at all
stinger.returnRateLabel: 76% of NFL players miss no time whatsoever
stinger.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence is the norm rather than the exception in contact sport
stinger.performanceLabel: Not measured; single events resolve before the next snap
stinger.careerImpact: A single stinger is nothing. Repeat episodes correlate with cervical stenosis — smaller Torg ratio in players with multiple episodes (0.75 against 0.87) — and that is what ends careers.
stinger.fantasyImpact: Almost never worth acting on. Three in four cost no time. The reason to care is a player with a history of them, where the pattern rather than the episode is the story.
stinger.sources: Epidemiology of Stingers in the National Football League 2015–2019 (2024); NFL Combine cervical spine injury history analysis; Brachial plexus injuries in the contact athlete: a narrative review, Annals of Joint
